Good Friday morning. This is Sam Francis.

DAN TO THE RESCUE: Keir Starmer’s grip on power this morning looks weaker than ever after John Healey’s resignation blew a hole through the PM’s strongest case for staying in No. 10: that in a dangerous world, he could still be trusted on national security. Healey’s central accusation, that Starmer had been “unable, and the Treasury unwilling” to fund the nation’s defense, was damaging enough on its own. But it was quickly followed by the resignations of Armed Forces Minister Al Carns and Healey’s PPSs Pamela Nash and Rachel Hopkins. With the Makerfield by-election and Andy Burnham’s expected return to parliament six days away, the threat to the prime minister feels close at hand. Dan Jarvis will need all the luck he can get.

Entering the lions’ den: Jarvis took up the poisoned chalice prestigious role of defense secretary at 9 p.m. and could have a hard landing. MoD officials confirmed late last night that his first outing will be a visit to the drone factory in Swindon later this morning— originally intended as the triumphant stage for the Defence Investment Plan launch, which now is presumably off, despite the fact that invites had already been sent out to major defense firms.

Watching brief: Plans were understandably in flux late last night as officials tried to salvage something presentable, with talk of a possible pooled camera and Jarvis potentially fronting up to the media in some form unconfirmed. FWIW, this is the same Swindon drone site my colleague Esther Webber reported last month had its opening held back so the prime minister could cut the ribbon alongside the DIP. The PM is no longer coming.

**A message from Palantir: At Palantir, what we value is helping our customers deliver better public services. Our software is driving up NHS operations, speeding up cancer diagnosis, tackling crime, preventing domestic violence and helping our armed forces protect our security. 17 per cent of our workforce is based here in the UK - and that’s what makes them tick.**

If anyone is able to ask Jarvis a question … they may well ask whether the DIP deal rejected by Healey is going ahead exactly as planned, or whether Jarvis accepted the job on the condition he could have a say on the detail (or at least read it top to bottom). Expect similar questions to Peter Kyle on the morning broadcast round and at the No. 10 Lobby briefing at 11.30 a.m.

DIP (probably) happens: The obvious clue in this is that No. 10 has rowed in hard behind the DIP as set out. In his exchange with Healey, Starmer insisted the current plan remained live, describing it as delivering “an unprecedented increase in defense spending in a sustainable way.” Exactly when anyone will actually see it, though, remains an open question ahead of next week’s G7 summit. And will any potential successor as PM stick to such a controversial plan? As Jessica Elgot points in the Guardian, Andy Burnham — should he make it from Wigan to SW1 — faces the exact same choices that drove Healey out. He’s not exactly put defense and foreign policy at the top of his pitches so far.

Healey big problem: The real hammer blow from Healey’s resignation was his implication that the prime minister wanted to give more funding to the Defence Investment Plan, but was too weak to pull rank on his chancellor. “This isn’t the beginning of the end, it has gone way beyond that,” one senior Labour adviser told the FT. Labour MP Graham Stringer told the Telegraph Starmer is a “dead prime minister walking.”

It’s just a flesh wound: Remember, Starmer wanted the DIP to be a central pillar of his legacy — a fully costed blueprint to show Labour was serious about the armed forces and that the U.K. was stepping up on the world stage. Instead, the plan’s credibility is now in tatters, despite Starmer wrestling somewhere between £10 billion and £13.5 billion from the Treasury — depending on who you listen to.

Can anyone solve it? But there is a deeper question as to whether any PM can produce a DIP that survives contact with the U.K.’s current finances while adequately girding us for a possible apocalypse. As the Guardian’s Pippa Crerar and Dan Sabbagh note, costs have spiraled under successive commitments from both Tory and Labour governments, compounded by longstanding weaknesses in MoD financial management. My colleague Emilio Casalicchio points out the original sin of the DIP was when the MoD discovered it had underestimated how much funding it needed as part of the Strategic Defence Review to the tune of £28 billion over four years. The Treasury found that figure simply unaffordable to find all at once and the haggling over that has led us here.

Although here’s a silver lining: Meg Hillier, the architect of last summer’s benefit cuts rebellion, told the i Paper’s Will Hazell that Labour MPs are now ready to back welfare reforms, following Alan Milburn’s youth joblessness review. Milburn himself is meeting a delegation from Singapore’s Ministry of Manpower in London today to learn why the NEET rate is 3.8 percent compared to Britain’s 13.5 percent.

Turner round for the books: Retired Air Marshal Andrew Turner told the FT the “DIP was unaffordable, which made it unannounceable” but argued it was “entirely plausible a new government and a new cabinet” might be able to make it work. Best of luck.

Brassed off: Do not rule out further departures today — albeit perhaps not from ministerial ranks. Chief of the Defence Staff Richard Knighton is now on “resignation watch,” according to the Daily Mail’s Jason Groves and Mark Nicol, after it emerged he had written directly to Starmer over concerns about funding for the DIP.

Straight out of central casting: One can only assume Knighton and the other chiefs will be on the blower to Jarvis, who arrived in Parliament in 2011 with what the BBC’s Brian Wheeler once dubbed “the dream CV” for a politician. Fourteen years in the Parachute Regiment, rising to major, an MBE and tours in Northern Ireland, Kosovo, Iraq, Afghanistan and Sierra Leone — before becoming the first officer since WWII to resign his commission to fight a by‑election in 2011. During the Corbyn years, he was often cast as the moderate the Tories would most fear. In the end, he sat out the leadership race, citing his young family.

Soft (boiled) power: Between 2018 and 2022 he also served as mayor of South Yorkshire, juggling the combined authority with his Commons role before giving up on double-jobbing and moving into government as security minister after the 2024 landslide. Those who played Playbook’s 2024 Christmas quiz will no doubt remember Jarvis also keeps rescue chickens, re-homed from the British Hen Welfare Trust, and brings eggs into Parliament to give as gifts. Perhaps he should start with the chiefs of the Army, Navy and RAF.

And why not give an egg to … Carns, who is on another interview round — this time post-resignation. He chatted to ITV’s Good Morning Britain a short time ago and should pop up on LBC at 7.20 a.m., the Today program at 8.10 a.m. and GB News at 8.45 a.m.

Time Healeys all wounds: Some observers have speculated Healey might want a tilt at the top job himself, although allies of Healey told the Sun there was “absolutely” no chance of him running for the Labour leadership. The Daily Mail hears the same. Though the Telegraph’s Ben Riley-Smith reckons Healey pulling the rug from under the PM — making him less able to contest any leadership challenge — could see the ex-defense secretary back in the MoD within weeks, should a leadership switch happen.

SCOOP — BLITZ SPIRIT: The prime minister is now facing the embarrassing prospect of explaining to allies at next week’s G7, including Donald Trump, why his own defense secretary felt he was not doing enough to keep his country safe. But international diplomacy also gives Starmer a chance to seize back some of the initiative. My colleague Esther Webber has caught a glimpse of internal documents showing the prime minister plans to roll out a blitz of announcements at the summit in France: on migration and Ukraine, as well as possible further Russian sanctions. In particular, she hears there could be a push to expand the U.K.’s Sandhurst deal with the French, designed to tackle small boats.

Trump card: The leaked details also suggest a coordinated effort to get Trump back on side in the run‑up to next month’s NATO summit in Ankara, with the push being led out of the U.K.’s Washington embassy. The U.S. president isn’t known for his love of NATO, nor does he tend to respond well to perceived pressure from allies — so, good luck, as they say, with that. Given the perceived wisdom in Westminster is that this may be Starmer’s final turn on the world stage, Playbook would gently suggest this could be the perfect chance for him to tell Trump what he really thinks. What could go wrong?

COOP, THERE IT IS: While the center of government continues in the trenches, the FCDO was keen to point out that Yvette Cooper is still working the diplomatic circuit, laying the groundwork for the G7. Cooper is in Paris to discuss Israel and Palestine with the French foreign secretary and civil society groups. Cooper announced sanctions on the settlers in the West Bank earlier in the week.

HEADACHE OF STATE: As flagged in yesterday morning’s lengthy spotted list, a fair chunk of Westminster — MPs, whips, No.10 staff, SpAds and, er, the Lobby — were out for a night full of cocktails on Wednesday. Playbook salutes everyone who got through yesterday’s avalanche of news nursing a hangover.

ALL QUIET ON THE WIGAN FRONT: The Labour and Reform campaigns in Makerfield are both hunkering down with no planned appearances today — but the most consequential by-election in a generation continues to make news.

SCOOP — SHIFTING FOCUS: A focus group for POLITICO in an Ashton-in-Makerfield pub has found Makerfield’s voters are angry and really want someone to feel their pain. And while some voters think Andy Burnham might make a difference, Reform UK and Nigel Farage are winning converts who want to  “shake up” the system.

Faith no more: Crime, immigration and the cost of living dominated concerns among a politically mixed group of voters — but the prevailing mood was one of deep cynicism. One participant, Bob, summed it up: in more than 90 years of voting, he had yet to encounter a “bloody good” politician. Read the full report by Tim Ross.

STICKING TO THE SCRIPT: The House Mag’s Sienna Rodgers has managed to get her hands on a Labour canvassing script that door-knockers are using in Makerfield, which intriguingly instructs them to say they are “out campaigning for Andy Burnham” rather than Labour. There are also several script cues that might raise eyebrows among Burnham’s soft-left power base, including telling potential voters that “Andy supports reducing net migration” and he believes “it is right to pursue root and branch reform” of the immigration system.

WIGAN OUT: Andy Burnham’s closest friends advised him to turn down the Makerfield seat, given how hard it looked to win, according to a fun deep-dive by the Guardian’s Jessica Elgot.

PARLIAMENT: Not sitting.

SCOOP —BANNED WAGON: My colleague Mizy Clifton has firmed up that the other pillar of Starmer’s legacy push, a ban on under-16s accessing social media, will be announced next week. Live-streaming, disappearing messages and functionalities that allow communication with adult strangers will also be banned for under-16s, and a social media curfew for 16-to-17-year-olds is also being considered. One slight snag: the definition of what counts as social media hasn’t yet been nailed down.

SCOOP — EARLY BIRDS: The Liberal Democrats are holding their first candidate “away day” today, training 28 prospective parliamentary candidates already picked for target seats. The party has moved earlier than ever on selections, part of a broader push to put itself on a more serious footing for a return to government. Playbook has been told Sheffield Hallam hopeful, 29-year-old councillor Sophie Crossthorn, recently named on the Sunday Times Young Power List, and South West Hertfordshire candidate Matt Sanders, a former Lib Dem adviser and one‑time sparring partner of Dominic Cummings during the coalition years.

Wetsuits at the ready: For more on how the Lib Dems have quietly rebuilt their press operation and central machine while Westminster tears itself apart (see previous newsletters for details), check out this long‑read by *checks notes* me. Anyone hoping that the Lib Dems getting serious about the next election means fewer Ed Davey stunts may want to look away now. The wetsuit is not going anywhere.

OWNING THE LIBS: Liberal think tank Bright Blue today publishes a cross-party essay collection arguing liberalism needs a reset after a populist decade. The book, including chapters from MPs like Liam Byrne, suggests a range of new policies, from ending the triple lock on pensions to introducing a “baby bonus” for all new parents and drilling for more north sea oil, to promoting Snus packets as an alternative to smoking cigarettes.

Fractured politics: Bright Blue is also hosting a talk at 3 p.m. with friend of the newsletter, psephologist Rob Ford, to discuss whether two-party politics is over.

UP CLOSE: Gary Klopfenstein, a U.S. fraudster accused of illicitly funding Robert Jenrick’s Conservative leadership campaign, met one of Jenrick’s current aides, Sam Armstrong, as part of a group to discuss the future of the Tory party before the alleged donations were made, the FT’s Rachel Rees reports. At the time, Klopfenstein had not been convicted of fraud. Jenrick’s lawyers told the FT the politician and his team complied with all electoral laws and Jenrick himself had no contact with Klopfenstein.

ON YER BIKE: Ministers want 60 percent of pupils in England cycling or walking to school by 2035 as part of Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander’s boost for active travel. The Guardian has a write-up.

CHAMPIONS! Economic Secretary to the Treasury Rachel Blake will announce in a speech to the Co-op Congress that she will appoint a champion for the co-op sector, with a recruitment process to follow.

WHAT THE GOVERNMENT WANTS TO TALK ABOUT: School students will learn how to plant a wildflower-friendly garden according to long-awaited plans for a natural history GCSE. The government has launched a 12-week consultation on the proposed subject content.

RETURNED: The party suspension of Lib Dem peer Chris Rennard has been lifted, as spotted by BylineTimes’ Josiah Mortimer. The peer had the whip removed in February after the party launched a new investigation into claims he sexually harassed female members. A Lib Dem spokesperson said the party’s independent complaints process decided to lift the suspension while their investigation is ongoing.

ENTERING THE RACE: Labour MP Steve Race is in discussions to take over the Labour Growth Group, my colleague Hannah Brenton reports. The MP for Exeter has floated taking the centrist group forward, after fellow MP Chris Curtis announced he was stepping down.

NOW LISTEN TO THIS: On this week’s episode of Westminster Insider, Sascha O’Sullivan asks: What is the point of political protest?

And keep your ears peeled For a bonus episode of Westminster Insider landing Sunday. Jack Blanchard was dragged away from his D.C. post by the tantalizing assignment of finding out who is the real Andy Burnham.

FUEL FOR THE WEEKEND: The King’s Birthday Honors list will be published on Saturday, with no doubt some political appointees. The Mirror’s Lizzy Buchan reports that Rugby Union star and motor neurone disease fundraiser Kevin Sinfield has been granted a knighthood.

THE KIDS AREN’T ALRIGHT: Young people are increasingly pessimistic about their future, with IPPR analysis finding that one in 14 young people believe they are likely to become long-term unemployed. This figure stood at just one in 50 in 2015.

SAFE AS HOUSES: Former Housing Secretary Angela Rayner is due to give a fireside chat from 3.50 p.m at the Propertymark One conference at Excel centre. Before she gets on stage Shadow Chancellor Mel Stride is due to give a speech, where he is expected to tell the room full of housing developers the Tory’s flagship plans to scrap stamp duty could mean 200,000 extra homes built over five years — a 25 percent boost on current building rates — based on modelling by the Adam Smith Institute.

COURT CIRCULAR: Four Palestine Action activists will be sentenced at 10 a.m. at Woolwich Crown Court after being found guilty of criminal damage at a U.K. site of Israel-based defense firm Elbit Systems. The hearing will see the judge decide whether there was a terrorism connection to their offense — despite the jury not being told of this possibility.

AND BREATHE: After two nights of chaos, protests held in some areas of Northern Ireland passed without incident following a “robust” police response, the BBC reports.

NUCLEAR OPTION: Donald Trump claimed that the U.S. has “ended the war” with Iran after asserting the two sides had agreed to a “very strong memorandum of understanding” including Tehran agreeing “never to have a nuclear weapon.” Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson has said the country did not yet reach a final decision on any agreement, according to state media. CNN has a live page covering the (ever-changing) details. Stop me if you think that you have heard this one before.

SCROOGE MCDUCK VIBES: Elon Musk is on the cusp of becoming the world’s first trillionaire as SpaceX debuts on the Nasdaq today at  a price of $135 a share. Fortune magazine has more on our brave new world.

BROMANCE: The World Cup is bringing together two potential 2028 presidential candidates  at Friday’s U.S. opener against Paraguay in LA, with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and California Gov. Gavin Newsom sitting in the same box at kickoff at SoFi Stadium. Romantic! My POLITICO colleagues have the deets.

WHO SMELT IT, DEALT IT: The Pentagon resumed “normal operations” on Thursday after part of the U.S. defense headquarters went into lockdown in response to what spokesperson Sean Parnell called an “air quality issue” that required “precautionary measures” while officials investigated. Subsequent testing, Parnell wrote on X, found no issues.

**A message from Palantir: Palantir software is helping to deliver better patient care - including 110,000 additional operations to date, a 15% reduction in discharge delays, a 6.8% increase in the number of patients finding out whether they need cancer treatment within 28 days, and the safe removal of 797,728 patients from waiting lists. The same software is helping police forces in England to tackle crime too. The Metropolitan Police have used it to identify misconduct within the force and arrest officers. It has helped Bedfordshire Police to reduce the time taken to check whether someone’s partner has a history of violence by 85 per cent, identifying 1,000 vulnerable women in a single year. It is also being used to bring organised crime gangs such as F*** the Police to justice. A stronger NHS and safer streets. Values we can all agree on.**

Westminster Insider: Westminster has seen it all when it comes to protests. This week Sascha O’Sullivan tries to find out the point of marching on Whitehall. She speaks to activist Peter Tatchell, former Conservative MP and gay rights campaigner Edwina Currie, Sophie Cowen, who spent years working for both Extinction Rebellion and Insulate Britain, and political scientist Maria Stephan.

Plus six of the best political podcasts for you to listen to this weekend …

PoliticsJoe Podcast: SDLP MP Claire Hanna joins to break down the recent violence and unrest in Northern Ireland.

Chopper’s Political Podcast: Father of the House Edward Leigh says the Tories and Reform UK must do an electoral pact, and Jess Asato joins to discuss her legal action against Grok AI.

SET TO RECORD: Reform UK Leader Nigel Farage has sat down with LBC’s Nick Ferrari for a special “Farage On the Record” programme airing at 9 p.m.

NEW GIG: RenewablesUK’s Barnaby Wharton is joining SHGH as Energy, Climate and Environment Director.
